To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
• Principal component analysis ( PCA ) is the eigendecomposition of a covariance matrix.
PCA is a technique for dimensionality reduction that is used for data compression and data visualization.
• The principal component of a set of points in a d-dimensional space is the line through the origin that best describes these points in a d − 1-dimensional subspace.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: Why and how does PCA work?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

PCA is an orthogonal linear transformation that transforms the data to a new coordinate system such that the greatest variance by some projection of the data comes to lie on the first coordinate (called the first principal component ), the second greatest variance on the second coordinate, and so on.
PCA can be used to reduce the dimensionality of data, while preserving as much information in the lower dimensional space as possible.

PCA is a linear transformation that transforms the original n observations of p variables into a new set of p variables which are linearly uncorrelated and are ordered so that the first few of these linearly uncorreleated variables taken together contain most of the variability present in all of the original variables.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a derivation of the principal component analysis algorithm, and we also provide a discussion of the algorithm and its singular value decomposition.
PCA is the optimal orthogonal projection of the data onto the subspace spanned by the principal components.
we derive PCA from the singular value decomposition of the data matrix.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PCA can be viewed as a singular value decomposition (SVD) of the data matrix.
PCA is a simple, elegant and powerful method for dimensionality reduction.
PCA is a linear projection that maps the original data into a lower dimensional space, while preserving the variance of the data as much as possible.
